extracted.intended_audience: farmers, rural householders, and rural engineers planning or constructing small-scale water supplies
extracted.subtask_description: Practical design and construction guidance for obtaining and protecting water supplies for an individual house or small community (springs, streams, reservoirs, dams, pipe lines, and pumping options). Emphasizes material choice, sizing, placement, and measures to avoid contamination and failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect springs from surface runoff and pollution
rubrics_metrics.description: If road or surface water carries pollution into the spring, another channel for the gulley water ought to be made, or the spring dug out and roofed over; when the spring is in a depression that collects surface drainage, protect the spring by a bank of earth and lead off drainage through a special pipe line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prevent contamination by diverting surface runoff away from the spring or by enclosing the spring; use earth banks and separate drains where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spring reservoir material and basic construction
rubrics_metrics.description: In protecting the spring and building up around it to put it underground, concrete is the most suitable material, although a large sewer pipe or a heavy cask or barrel will answer the purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dig the spring to about four or five feet and use pumping or temporary drains while building concrete walls; leave holes on the side from which the spring water comes; connect openings to agricultural tile drains to increase yield and drain ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide inflow openings on the side of spring water entry
rubrics_metrics.description: In building walls, it is important to notice from which side the spring water comes, and on that side holes should be left in the wall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These openings may be connected with tile drains laid out from the spring in different directions to both drain the ground and add volume to the spring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporary drainage during spring-chamber construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of pumping out water during construction, where the ground slopes rapidly one can carry out a drainpipe from the lowest level; this drain is to be later stopped up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use gravity drainage where possible to avoid constant pumping during construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spring reservoir sizing relative to flow and consumption
rubrics_metrics.description: The size of the spring reservoir depends on the average rate of flow of the spring and on the quantity of water used; if there is always an overflow no large storage is needed, but if the spring is low at times storage must be allowed for.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate daily consumption (example: family of ten might use 500 gallons/day). For most exacting conditions one day's supply suffices (example chamber four feet deep and 4x5 feet area ≈ 500 gal). If spring supply < consumption, compute basin capacity from required days' storage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increase spring yield with drain-tile
rubrics_metrics.description: Possibility of increasing the yield of the spring by laying draintile in a ditch running along the permeable stratum; these pipes may run fifty or one hundred feet each way from the main spring so long as they continue to find ground water.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tile drains radiating from the spring to tap additional groundwater.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spring-reservoir wall thickness by depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Walls of spring reservoirs for depths of six to eight feet need not be more than nine inches thick, whether brick or concrete; greater depths should increase thickness to twelve inches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Increase wall thickness as depth increases to maintain structural integrity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spring-chamber roof and reinforcement specifications
rubrics_metrics.description: For spans up to ten feet make the roof a flat slab of concrete six inches thick, imbedding one-half-inch iron rods spaced about a foot apart each way and extending into the side walls; increase rod size with span (three-quarter-inch up to nine-foot span, one-inch up to twelve-foot span).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer concrete slab roofs over plank; for access provide a corner opening/manhole with side walls carried up above ground and an iron cover that can be locked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide outlet and drainage in spring-chamber
rubrics_metrics.description: Besides the outlet pipe (placed about halfway between top and bottom for best water) there should be a drainpipe from the lowest part of the enclosure with a valve reachable through a valve box; consider twofold chambers to allow inspection at any time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan positions of drain, house pipe, and collection pipes before pouring walls—easier to leave holes than to dig through concrete later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete mix for spring reservoirs
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete should be of good quality: one part of cement to five parts of gravel or to four parts of stone and two parts of sand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A concrete bottom is sometimes used but not necessary; ensure correct mix and embedments to avoid leaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stream intake placement to avoid freezing
rubrics_metrics.description: If stream volume exceeds maximum consumption, carry the intake pipe out under water and protect with a strainer; but since streams may freeze down to the strainer, place the intake in a pool deep enough that it never freezes (sometimes create a pool for this purpose).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If storage is used, place intake at least two feet below surface of water.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to build a dam for stream supply
rubrics_metrics.description: If stream is not deep or minimum flow is inadequate for maximum needs, a dam across the stream becomes a necessity; several dam types are suitable depending on conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select dam type based on depth, flow, valley geometry, and available materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dirt dam considerations and slope/base requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Dirt dams are not generally desirable if overflow must run over the dam unless crest is protected; if a dirt dam is used, slope on each face should be at least two feet horizontal for every foot in height (e.g., a 10-foot high dam needs at least 45-foot base width).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use masonry core or protective crest to prevent washout; ensure adequate slope and base width for stability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timber plank core dam construction
rubrics_metrics.description: A very good dam can be made by driving 3-inch tongue-and-grooved planking tight across a gulley and then filling in on each side, ensuring appropriate face slopes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This method gives a central timber core with earth on sides; slope requirement as above.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concrete or stone core dam preference and foundation needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Second type replaces timber core with a thin concrete wall (6–12 inches) or stone masonry light wall held by earth fill; concrete is preferable for water-tightness. The problem is ensuring a foundation that prevents leakage under the dam; ideal foundation is rock.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where soft or permeable banks exist, carry a cut-off wall (about 12 inches thick) well into the bank (≈10 feet each side) and down until it reaches impermeable stratum to shut off leakage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative cheap stone-dumping dam method
rubrics_metrics.description: Damming by continual dumping of field stone into a brook will settle into a slope and silt will fill holes, eventually becoming practically water-tight; protect top stones with a plank crest if floods run over the dam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cheap but requires protecting crest from erosion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arch dam in narrow gorge option
rubrics_metrics.description: In a narrow gorge with rock sides it is possible to use an upstream arch dam whose resistance is provided by abutment action of rock sides; for a 10-foot dam the curved dam thickness might be ~12 inches while gravity dam would be 3–4 feet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arch dams require superior workmanship despite saving materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent erosion at dam toe by shaping downstream face
rubrics_metrics.description: Never allow water falling over the dam to fall directly on the ground in front; make the lower section curved so the water leaves horizontally rather than vertically, and consider a plank floor or stilling pool below the dam.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide curved downstream section or still pool to dissipate energy and avoid undermining the dam.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious with brush and crib dams
rubrics_metrics.description: Brush dams (interwoven branches) and crib dams (log cribs filled with stone) have been used but are not permanent and their construction expense may approach that of permanent structures; generally not recommended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use only when cost/availability justify and when permanence is not required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waste weir sizing by watershed area and weir depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Capacity of waste weirs depends on flood-water volume which depends on watershed area; maximum run-off in eastern U.S. small areas ≈100 cubic feet per second per square mile. For a depth of 1 foot use factor 30 feet of weir per square mile; depth 2 ft factor 10; depth 3 ft factor 6; depth 4 ft factor 4.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 12 sq. mile watershed => for 1 ft depth need 360 ft weir, for 2 ft need 120 ft, for 3 ft need 72 ft, for 4 ft need 48 ft. Proper weir design and erosion resistance are critical to prevent dam washout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waste weir location relative to valley width and watershed
rubrics_metrics.description: When valley is narrow and watershed large the waste weir may occupy whole width of dam, requiring masonry construction; when watershed small and valley wide make weir only a portion of dam width and make remainder masonry or earth as convenient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match weir placement and dam construction type to topography and watershed size.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gate house necessity and intake pipe placement
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a gate house (masonry or wooden manhole) at the back of the dam where the outlet pipe passes and put a gate or valve to shut off water; intake pipe end should be placed about two feet above the bottom of the pond rather than resting in the mud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow valves reachable from surface (valve box) and consider admitting water from different reservoir levels in larger installations to obtain best quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pipe line material selection and trade-offs
rubrics_metrics.description: Pipe lines may be hollow wooden logs, vitrified tile, cast-iron pipe, wrought-iron pipe, and lead pipe; lead is expensive and wooden is short-lived; cast-iron not made in small sizes so tile or wrought-iron remain practical choices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose material based on size needed, cost, durability, and pressure; tile is cheaper but joints are harder to make watertight and impractical over ~10 ft pressure; iron for pressured runs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vitrified tile pipe and joint-making guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Vitrified tile (6-inch diameter suggested for open-ditch replacement) prevents surface pollution and costs about ten cents/ft; joints in tile pipe must be carefully made and packed with cement (not merely plastered) to be watertight, especially in small diameters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thoroughly fill joints with not-very-wet cement and ram/pack into every part of the joint; four-inch tile is possible but requires more care than six-inch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for friction losses and choose pipe diameter accordingly
rubrics_metrics.description: In flowing through a small pipe, water loses much head by friction which increases rapidly with velocity; using too small a pipe to save money can reduce delivered water to a dribble over long runs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid undersizing; consider required flow (example: to supply three faucets at reasonable rate need ≈2000 gallons/day or ~1.5 gallons/minute) and choose diameter to keep friction losses acceptable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic comparison of pipe materials (costs per running foot)
rubrics_metrics.description: Cost of cast-iron pipe should not be more than $0.30/ft for 4-inch and $0.50/ft for 6-inch plus lead per joint; terra-cotta pipe is cheaper and may be worth careful jointing to substitute for iron.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor material and jointing costs when selecting pipe type for long runs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer gravity supply over pumping when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Proper method is to make use of pond or stream at such elevation that water will flow to the house by gravity when possible; gravity supply has negligible daily maintenance charges and greater reliability than pumps which require daily fuel and repair.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare long-term maintenance costs and reliability: small daily pumping expense accumulates interest equivalent; gravity supply often preferable even if initial cost is higher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider pump capital vs operating costs
rubrics_metrics.description: One pump may cost more initially but save on fuel/repairs making it economical over time; example given comparing $0.10/day fuel cost and interest equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When choosing pumps, weight initial cost against likely operating expense and maintenance; sometimes borrowing to obtain a gravity supply is cheaper long-term than running a pump.

rubrics_metrics.name: Windmill suitability and sizing
rubrics_metrics.description: Windmills can be cheapest power for pumping but depend on wind; they require large storage to cover calm periods, and a 12-foot mill minimum is recommended; wind must blow 12–16 mph for efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use steel construction, strong foundation and anchoring; locate to receive prevailing winds and account for storm loads; consider frost dangers when locating tank on tower versus attic storage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hydraulic ram suitability and flow/head ratio
rubrics_metrics.description: Hydraulic ram is cheapest method of pumping provided sufficient flow with head is available; it requires about seven times as much water to flow through the ram and be wasted as is pumped (i.e., large throughput needed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disadvantages: fall not always obtainable, stream flow may be insufficient, action subject to interruptions from air accumulation and ice; advantage: no attendance and negligible maintenance. Rams can operate against large heads but are sensitive to discharge pipe length (friction reduces pumped amount if >100 ft). Manufacturer tables (sizes, required drive-pipe sizes, least feet of fall, capacities, prices) guide selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of securing fall for hydraulic rams
rubrics_metrics.description: Two methods: long drive pipe from higher level to ram without a drain pipe, or placing the ram in intermediate position with considerable lengths of each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose method based on site topography and available fall; see diagrams for layouts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other mechanical power options and limitations (water wheels, hot-air engines, gas engines, steam pumps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Bucket water wheels may be used but small streams often run dry; Rider-Ericsson hot-air engines run on various fuels with moderate fuel consumption; gas (or oil) engines are efficient and versatile; steam pumps sensible if boiler already exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select engine/pump type based on existing equipment, fuel availability, required capacity, and desire to use engine for other tasks. Tables of capacities, fuel consumption, and costs are provided to inform selection (examples and manufacturer data included).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hot-air engine pump sizing and fuel consumption data
rubrics_metrics.description: Table provided showing cylinder sizes (5" to 10"), suction/discharge pipe sizes, capacities per hour, cu. ft. of gas, kerosene per hour, anthracite coal per hour, and price—used to evaluate hot-air engines for pumping.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use manufacturer data to assess required size and operating cost; example: 5" size gives 150 gal/hr and ~1 qt kerosene/hr with $90 price.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gas engine suitability and multipurpose use
rubrics_metrics.description: Gas engines (including gasolene-fueled) are effective small-power devices from 0.5 to 20 H.P.; can be used for pumping, driving dynamos, or other farm machinery, and an ordinary laborer with instruction can operate them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Often arrange belt shifting so the engine can drive pump or dynamo; oil engines (kerosene) may be safer than gasolene engines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steam pumps useful when a boiler already exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a steam pump for a single house is not usually considered unless a small boiler is already installed for other uses (dairy, silage); in that case a small duplex pump can be connected and used for water supply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider combined uses of boiler to justify steam pump; tables provide pump capacities for various cylinder sizes and pipe sizing guidance.
